question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- y=3 \cdot y^{2} \cdot e^{\left(x-6\right)}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x-6\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-1\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot e^{\left(x-6\right)}\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(1\right)z=- 3 \cdot e^{\left(x-6\right)}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{\left(x-6\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{\left(x-6\right)}\,z\right)=- 3 \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{\left(x-6\right)}z=- \frac{3 \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}}{2}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{- \left(x-6\right)} - \frac{3 \cdot e^{\left(x-6\right)}}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{2 \cdot e^{\left(x-6\right)}}{2 \cdot C - 3 \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=1\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot \left(x-6\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-2\right)z=- 6 \cdot \left(x-6\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -2\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}\,z\right)=- 6 \cdot \left(x-6\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}z=3 \cdot \left(\left(x-6\right) + \frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)} + 3 \cdot \left(x-6\right) + \frac{3}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2}{2 \cdot C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)} + 6 \cdot \left(x-6\right) + 3}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.

\left(x+6\right)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+3 \cdot y=- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2} \cdot y^{\frac{3}{4}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+6\right)>0$. Take $y>0$. For even powers and powers of $2/3$ in the choices, retain only intervals where the base is positive. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, rearrange and divide by the coefficient of the derivative:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+\frac{3 \cdot y}{\left(x+6\right)}=- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right) \cdot y^{\frac{3}{4}}. $$

This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=\frac{3}{\left(x+6\right)}\\ q(x)&=- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)\\ n&=\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{\frac{3}{4}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{1}{4}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{4 \cdot y^{\frac{3}{4}}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(\frac{3}{4 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}\right)z=- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}{4}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int \frac{3}{4 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x}=\left(x+6\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\left(x+6\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}\,z\right)=- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{\frac{7}{4}}}{4}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$\left(x+6\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}z=- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{\frac{11}{4}}}{11}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{C}{\left(x+6\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}} - \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}}{11}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{1}{4}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(\frac{C}{\left(x+6\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}} - \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}}{11}\right)^{4}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. The displayed expression for $z$ must be positive because $z=y^{\frac{1}{4}}>0$.
